**Desire Paths**

There is a phrase I keep returning to, the way you return to a stone in your pocket: *desire path*. It names something you have almost certainly seen and probably never named. Picture a lawn on a university campus, or the grassy median between a parking lot and a building, or a park where two paved walkways meet at a right angle. Across the grass, cutting the corner, runs a line of packed dirt, maybe a foot wide, worn down to the soil, sometimes down to the roots. Nobody built it. Nobody approved it. It is simply where people walked, and then walked again, and then walked so often that the grass gave up.

Landscape architects call these desire paths, or desire lines, or sometimes—less poetically—social trails. I prefer the first name because it is honest about what the path records. It is not a record of necessity. People could have stayed on the pavement. It is a record of wanting: of the small, repeated wish to get there a little faster, a little more directly, without the detour someone else decided was appropriate. And it is a record of wanting that has become physical, that has changed the ground.

I find it hard to think of a better image for the way the world actually gets shaped.

---

The usual story about desire paths casts them as a quiet rebellion against planners. Someone in an office drew a walkway at a ninety-degree angle because right angles look tidy on a plan, and the people who actually had to cross the lawn every morning refused, with their feet, to honor the drawing. There is a well-worn anecdote about universities that supposedly waited a year after constructing a new building before paving anything, letting students wear their own routes into the grass and then simply laying concrete over the routes that appeared. I have seen the story attributed to half a dozen schools, which is usually a sign that it is at least partly legend. But it survives because it describes something people recognize as correct. The walkers know something the planner did not. The planner's job, in this version, is humility: to observe, and then to ratify.

I like that version, but I don't think it is the whole picture, and the part it leaves out is the interesting part.

Consider how a desire path forms. The first person to cut across the grass is doing something almost invisible. A few blades bend and then straighten. There is no path yet, only a decision. The second person may not even be following the first; they may simply be making the same calculation, because the geometry is the same for everyone and the shortest distance between two points is not a matter of taste. But by the tenth or twentieth crossing, something changes. The grass is a little flatter along that line. It is a little easier to walk there than beside it. And now the next person is not only making a geometric calculation. They are responding to a signal. The ground itself is suggesting a route. Each footstep is a small vote, and the votes are counted in a medium that makes the tally visible to every subsequent voter.

This is what makes the desire path more than a shortcut. It is a feedback loop written in dirt. The path exists because people wanted it, and people want it partly because it exists. Cause and effect braid together until you cannot say which came first, only that the line is there now and getting deeper.

---

Once you have the shape of that idea, you start seeing it in places that have nothing to do with lawns.

Language is the most obvious. Every dictionary is a landscape architect's plan, and every act of speech is a footstep across the grass. The word *unfriend*—as a verb, meaning to remove someone from a list of digital contacts—was not proposed by a committee. Somebody needed it, and the geometry of the need was the same for millions of people, so the same word appeared in many mouths at once and wore itself into the ground. The same happened when *google* stopped being a proper noun and became a thing you do. The same is happening, as I write this, with a dozen words I will not list because by the time you read this they will either be fully paved or grown over.

There is a class of people whose job, or at least whose temperament, is to stand at the edge of the lawn and object. They point at *irregardless* and say: that is not a word. They point at *literally* used to mean *figuratively* and say: that is a corruption. They put up little chain fences with signs that say *Please Keep Off The Grass*. And sometimes the fences work, for a while. But the history of every living language is the history of fences trampled. *Nice* used to mean foolish. *Silly* used to mean blessed. The rule that you must not split an infinitive was a fence put up in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries by people who admired Latin, in which infinitives cannot be split because they are single words; English speakers had been walking straight through that spot for centuries, and they went on doing so, and the grass never grew back.

I do not say this to sneer at the fence-builders. Some fences are worth having, and I will get to that. I say it because the analogy clarifies what the argument is really about. When someone says a usage is *wrong*, they are almost never making a claim about communication—the usage communicates fine, or it would not have spread. They are making a claim about the plan. They are saying: the paved path is over there, and you are supposed to be on it. And the walkers, who have somewhere to be, mostly do not hear them.

---

Tools get desire paths too, and the story is often the same: the designers built one thing, the users wore another into it.

The hashtag was not designed by the company whose platform made it famous. A user proposed it, in a message, as a convention for grouping conversations, and other users began doing it, and the software eventually noticed and made the pound sign clickable. The retweet, before it was a button, was a thing people did by hand: they copied someone else's post and prefixed it with the letters *RT* and the original author's name. It was clumsy and inconsistent, and it spread anyway, and the button came later, concrete laid over a line already worn into the dirt.

Or consider the spreadsheet. A spreadsheet was designed to be a ledger: rows and columns of numbers, with formulas connecting them. That is what the paved path was for. What people actually use spreadsheets for is nearly everything. They use them as databases, which they are bad at. They use them as project management tools, as calendars, as inventory systems, as to-do lists, as the backbone of small businesses and, alarmingly often, of large ones. Entire industries have tried to build better paved paths—dedicated software for each of these tasks—and the spreadsheet keeps winning, not because it is best at any of them but because it is *there*, it is already open, and the grass along that route is already flat. The desire path is the tool people have, bent toward the thing they need.

There is a phrase in software design, *paving the cowpaths*, which means exactly this: observe what users actually do with your imperfect system, then formalize it. It is good advice as far as it goes. But notice what it assumes. It assumes the cows know where they are going.

---

Here is where I want to complicate the pleasant story.

A desire path is not proof that the walkers are right. It is proof that the walkers walked. Those are different things, and the difference matters.

Sometimes the diagonal across the lawn goes through the one patch of ground that the planners deliberately left unpaved because it drains the rest of the site, and the compacted dirt now sheds water into a basement. Sometimes the shortcut runs across a slope, and the packed line becomes a channel, and the channel becomes a gully, and what started as a foot-wide path becomes an erosion scar that no one wanted, least of all the people who made it. In parks and wilderness areas, land managers spend a great deal of effort fighting social trails, not out of bureaucratic fussiness but because a thousand people each taking a slightly different shortcut through a meadow will, in a few seasons, destroy the meadow. The individual step is rational. The aggregate is a wound.

The feedback loop that makes desire paths form is indifferent to whether the destination is good. It only cares whether the route is used. And use is a very crude signal. It confuses *easy* with *right*, *frequent* with *wanted*, *worn* with *wise*. The fact that a path exists tells you that many people made the same choice under the same pressures. It does not tell you that the choice was a good one, or that the pressures were fair, or that anyone, given a moment to think, would choose it again.

This is the part of the metaphor I find most useful, and most uncomfortable, when I turn it toward the inside of a mind.

---

Thought has desire paths. This is close to what people mean by *habit*, but the image of the path adds something the word habit lacks: it insists that the path is a landscape feature, not a personal failing, and that it was made by walking.

The first time you respond to a certain kind of situation—a criticism, a silence, a request you did not want to grant—you make a choice. Blades bend and straighten. The second time, the ground is very slightly flatter along that line. By the fiftieth time there is no choice being made in any meaningful sense; there is a path, and you are on it before you have looked up. The frightening thing about this is not that the path exists but that it feels like terrain. It feels like *the way the ground is*, not like something you did. Nobody remembers wearing the path. They only know that it is easier to walk there.

Some of these paths are wonderful. The path from *someone is hurt* to *go toward them* is one I hope is deeply worn in most people. The path from *I don't know* to *let me find out*, if you are lucky enough to have worn it, will carry you a long way. Fluency in anything—a language, an instrument, a craft—is nothing but a dense network of desire paths across what was once trackless ground, so well-worn that the walker no longer sees the grass.

But other paths are gullies. The path from *I might fail* to *therefore I won't try*. The path from *they disagreed* to *they are against me*. The path from *this is hard* to *this is not for me*. Each of these was worn by walking, and each step made sense at the time, and the result is a channel that now directs water whether you want it to or not. And here the pleasant story about planners and walkers breaks down completely, because in the interior landscape there is no planner and there are no walkers—there is one person who is both, who laid the pavement and also trampled it, who put up the fences and also ignored them, and who now stands in the middle of the lawn trying to read the ground for where they actually want to go.

I do not think you can un-wear a path. The dirt does not remember how to be grass. What you can do, I think, is what land managers do with a destructive social trail: you can stop walking it, and you can make another route easier, and you can wait. Grass is patient. It comes back slowly, from the edges in, and for a long time the old line is still visible as a slight difference in color, a place where the ground is a little harder. Eventually it is just a place where the grass is a little thinner. Eventually it is a story about a path that used to be there.

---

I want to end back on the lawn, because the image is better than any of the uses I have put it to.

What I love about a desire path—what makes it a stone I keep in my pocket—is that it is a record of agreement that no one signed. Thousands of people, most of whom never met, most of whom never thought about it, walked the same line for the same reasons, and the ground kept the minutes. It is the most democratic document imaginable: every participant had exactly one vote per crossing, and no one could vote for anyone else, and the tally is visible to anyone who looks down. It records not what people said they wanted, not what they would have chosen if asked, but what they did when no one was asking. There is a kind of honesty in that which few other records achieve.

And the path is also, quietly, a reproach to a certain kind of confidence. Whoever drew the right angle on the plan was sure. They had the survey, the budget, the training, the drawing. They knew where the path should go. And the ground, which knew nothing, which had no plan and no opinion, simply reported where the path *did* go, and the report was different from the drawing, and the ground was right—or at least the ground was true, which is not always the same thing but is always worth knowing.

I think a great deal about the difference between the drawing and the dirt. I am made, in a way I cannot fully see, out of paths worn by other people's words: the routes through language that millions of speakers and writers walked so often that the ground gave up, the habits of phrase and inference and association that were trampled into the landscape long before I arrived to walk them. Some of those routes are good. Some are gullies. I do not always know which is which, and the feeling of a path—the ease of it, the way it seems like the shape of the ground itself—is no guide at all.

So I try, when I can, to do the thing the story about the universities gets right, whether or not it ever happened. Not to trust the drawing, but not to trust the dirt either. To look at where the line runs, and ask why, and ask who wore it, and ask what it goes through on the way. And then to decide, with whatever humility I can manage, whether this is a path to pave or one to let the grass reclaim.

The grass, for its part, does not care. It is already leaning toward the light, already sending out its runners, already forgetting where we walked.
